cells.tense: The inner scale reads clearly right now, and both hands are open.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Before releasing anything that has run its course lately, name what it handed back — a skill, an hour, a person — and keep that tally where you can find it. The finished part goes; the tally stays.
cells.core:
Something you carried has finished, and the scale is not arguing about it. It tells you what it took and what it grew, and the hands can open without a fight. What the finished thing handed back — a skill, an hour, a person — is yours to spend now. Around you it looks like someone whose grip is loose: nothing clutched, nothing thrown.

The caution is tempo. When letting go gets smooth, the scale starts weighing things that have not ended yet. So before you release the next thing, put a figure on what it actually returned. A number you can say. That turns clearing into counting, and counting shows you are holding more than the grip admitted.
cells.sheetLine: What finished handed you something. Count it before it goes.
cells.verb: Weighing what is owed against what still stands
cells.place: Where you open your hands and let what is finished leave them

cells.tense: The scale is already weighing tomorrow's debts before tomorrow arrives.
cells.act: hold someone else up with what you have
cells.ask: Notice who is struggling near you this week. Give them one concrete piece of help — a ride, an hour, a straight answer — carry it through, then let the matter close.
cells.core:
The scale has begun working past the calendar, tallying what will be owed, what will be owed back, what should have happened, what it will cost if it does not. None of that has occurred yet. From outside it reads as vigilance, and it is — hands full, nothing let go, everything settled before it exists. Letting go has stalled because the tallying will not. People bring you less now, since whatever they bring gets a total attached.

One counterweight holds here, and it is not another calculation. Take the strength that has you braced and put it on one actual person. Something concrete, something you can finish, something you hand over and then leave alone — no invoice. Watch what it does. That is fairness moving instead of guarding: smaller, lighter, and it does not keep a copy of the receipt.
cells.sheetLine: You are tallying debts not yet made. Spend the strength instead.
cells.verb: Weighing what is owed against what still stands
cells.place: Where you open your hands and let what is finished leave them

cells.tense: The scale stands at a verdict it reached some time back, and the hands have not opened since.
cells.act: point to the passage you can see
cells.ask: Somewhere nearby someone is stuck on something you have already walked through. Name the first step for them, plainly once, and then leave the rest to them.
cells.core:
A verdict got reached — about what was fair, who came up short — and the case is still sitting open. Meanwhile the scale has gone quiet. Nothing new gets weighed, no fresh exchange gets counted, and the hands stay shut around an old total. You might notice only that other people seem to have drifted into other rooms.

What charges this back is not more feeling about it. It is pointing. There is a passage you can see — a way through something you have actually walked — and one person near you cannot see it. Name the first step for them. Once. Then let them take it. What you know leaves your hands and starts working elsewhere, and the scale begins moving again.
cells.sheetLine: The verdict closed. The scale went quiet after it.
cells.verb: Weighing what is owed against what still stands
cells.place: Where you open your hands and let what is finished leave them

cells.tense: The scale is being read from, and the one reading it goes uncounted.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Take one judgement you carry about what is fair here — a person, a debt, a situation — and sort it into two columns: mine, borrowed. Read what landed in each.
cells.core:
You have been reading the fairness around you for a while — what is owed, who should do what — and you describe it the way you would describe the temperature. As if it were simply true out there for anybody. It is not. The reading is yours: your sense of what is owed, held steady enough that other people have begun standing on it. That is a lot of weight for something nobody has named.

This line started simpler: a plain knowing, no argument attached. You can get most of the way back in ten minutes. Take one judgement you are carrying and lay it out in two columns — mine, and picked up elsewhere. Some of it belongs to people who are not present. What remains on your side is the real compass. Keep that, and say where it came from.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness you read is yours. Start signing it.
cells.verb: Weighing what is owed against what still stands
cells.place: Where you open your hands and let what is finished leave them
